title: Block lists miss most AI-crawler limits: 80% come from path rules, not blocks
why: Expected: a block list decides AI access. Found: in our July sample only 2% of AI-crawler pairs were blocked outright, while 80% were limited by a Disallow rule on an ordinary path.

drafts.text: A block list is the wrong unit. In our July sample of 219 hand-picked homepages, 2% of AI-crawler pairs were blocked outright. 80% were limited by a Disallow rule, usually on an ordinary path. Check the path, not the bot name.

A piece this week argues that blocking an AI training crawler is not the same as blocking a retrieval bot. The distinction holds. Our own data suggests the bigger gap sits elsewhere.

In July we scanned 219 hand-picked homepages against ten AI crawlers: 2,190 site and crawler pairs. Only 2% were blocked outright. About 80% were limited by a Disallow rule, usually on an ordinary path, and 18% were open.

So the block list is rarely the whole story. The path rule is what matters. A line written for one section of a site can reach every bot that reads robots.txt.

Monday morning: list the user agents your robots.txt names, then check which paths each one cannot reach.

Method note: 219 homepages scanned 29 to 31 July 2026. Hand-picked, not a random sample, one scan each. Crawler access results published 5 October 2026. This measures readiness, not citations.
